newsitem.title: USA: Senators hear Huang funneled $50,000 to Democrats.
newsitem.headline: Senators hear Huang funneled $50,000 to Democrats.

text.p: A U.S. Senate committee probing campaign finance abuses heard evidence on Tuesday that Asian-American businessman John Huang helped funnel $50,000 to the Democratic Party from a giant Indonesian company friendly to President Bill Clinton.
But a witness who worked in an office next door to Huang's dismissed Republican suggestions that Huang might have been a spy for Indonesia's Lippo Group or the Chinese government.

"I think the answer to the claims, if I may, is hogwash," Harold Arthur, chairman of the board of directors of the Los Angeles-based Lippo Bank, told the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee as it opened its second week of hearings.

Asked why Lippo Bank owner James Riady, a longtime friend of Clinton, would contribute about $800,000 to the Democratic National Committee and various state Democratic organisations, Arthur said: "Friendship."
Arthur, while admitting he was a "good Republican," said he doubted the Riadys made the contributions seeking any kind of special favours.

The committee heard testimony and examined documents showing that in 1992 the Lippo Group reimbursed an American subsidiary for a $50,000 contribution to the Democratic National Committee in August 1992.

The reimbursement was sought by Huang, who was then an executive of the Los Angeles-based subsidiary, Hip Hing Holdings, a money-losing operation whose sole asset was a parking lot worth several million dollars.

Huang, a former Commerce Department official who Clinton and others pushed to have hired as a DNC fund-raiser for the 1996 election cycle, is accused by Republicans of raising hundreds of thousands of dollars in illegal political contributions, allegedly of foreign origin.

The committee also made public a document that showed a China-born British citizen, Eric Hotung of Hong Kong, promised a $100,000 contribution to the Democrats in 1995 in exchange for a meeting with Clinton national security aides to seek "a higher profile for Taiwan on the world stage."

"Mr. Hotung has several policy options that he would like to suggest for consideration by administration officials," said a Sept. 20, 1995, memo from Democratic National Committee co-chair Don Fowler to White House political aide Doug Sosnik.

The 16-member committee chaired by Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson heard from a former Hip Hing officer, Juliana Utomo, who worked for Huang and said she signed the $50,000 check for the DNC at the request of Huang or another officer without knowing what the DNC was.

Days later, Huang sent a request to Lippo's Jakarta headquarters seeking a wire transfer of $146,500. It specifically cited the $50,000 to the DNC Victory Fund as an expense for which reimbursement was sought.

"There's a pretty clear document here requesting a reimbursement for a $50,000 donation to the DNC Victory Fund, which certainly looks like the movement of foreign money into an American campaign in 1992," observed Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat.

Thompson began his hearings saying that evidence given to the committee indicated China had a plan and may still have a plan to influence U.S. elections. He said the plan was inspired by the perception that Taiwan, which Beijing considers a part of China, had increased its own influence in Congress.

Democrats who believe Thompson is on a partisan witch hunt insisted they had seen the same material as Thompson but did not come to the same conclusion. However, Thompson was backed on Tuesday by Lieberman after CIA and FBI officials briefed committee members privately on Monday.
